subject: biology
title: Cell theory and cell types
summary: The three ideas of cell theory, how prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (and plant and animal cells) differ, and why surface area to volume ratio limits how big a cell can be.
body:
Every living thing, from a bacterium in yoghurt to a gum tree to you, is made of cells. Cell theory is the starting point for all of biology, because it tells us that the cell is the smallest thing that can be truly alive. In this lesson you will learn the main types of cells, how to tell them apart, and why cells are so small.

## Think of it like this

### Prokaryotes are a studio flat, eukaryotes are a house with rooms

A **prokaryotic cell** is like a one-room studio flat: the bed, kitchen and desk are all in one open space. Its **DNA** just sits in one area of the **cytosol** (the **nucleoid**), with no walls around it. A **eukaryotic cell** is like a big house with separate rooms and doors. The DNA is locked away in its own room, the **nucleus**, and other jobs happen in their own rooms, the **membrane-bound organelles** such as mitochondria. Both homes still have the basics everyone needs: walls to the outside (the **plasma membrane**), and a kitchen to make things (the **ribosomes**).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a studio flat is not "less alive" than a house; prokaryotes are not simpler leftovers but hugely successful cells, and they still have some internal organisation without membrane rooms.

### Surface area to volume ratio is like a school canteen

Picture a canteen with one serving window. When the school has 50 students, everyone gets lunch quickly. If the school grows to 1000 students but the canteen only adds a couple more windows, the queue gets huge. The windows are the **surface area** (the membrane where things get in and out) and the students are the **volume** (the cytoplasm that needs supplying). As a cell grows, its volume grows faster than its surface area, so its **surface area to volume ratio** (SA:V) falls and supply cannot keep up. The fix is the same as for a big school: run lots of small canteens (lots of small cells), or make the building long and thin with windows all along it (flattened cells or **microvilli**).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* students choose to queue, but molecules move by diffusion and transport through the membrane, and distance to the centre of the cell matters too, not just the number of "windows".

### In real life

Many antibiotics work because bacteria are prokaryotes. For example, penicillin stops bacteria building the peptidoglycan in their **cell wall**, and human cells have no such wall, so the drug harms the bacteria far more than us. Your lungs and small intestine are packed with tiny folds and sacs for the same SA:V reason that cells stay small.

## Key ideas

### Cell theory

**Cell theory** is one of the core ideas of biology. It has three parts:

1. All living things are made of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
3. All cells come from pre-existing cells, by cell division.

The third point matters because it rules out the old idea that life could appear from non-living matter (called **spontaneous generation**). A new cell is only ever made when an existing cell divides.

Cell theory was only possible once microscopes were good enough to see cells. Most cells are measured in **micrometres** (µm). One micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre (1 mm = 1000 µm).

### Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

All cells share four features: a **plasma membrane** that separates the inside from the outside, **cytosol** (the watery fluid inside), **ribosomes** to make proteins, and **DNA** as the genetic material. Beyond that, cells fall into two big groups.

**Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA sits in a region of the cytosol called the **nucleoid**. Key features:

- A single, circular chromosome, often with small extra rings of DNA called **plasmids**.
- Smaller ribosomes than eukaryotes.
- Usually a **cell wall** outside the plasma membrane (in bacteria this contains peptidoglycan).
- Some have a **capsule**, **flagella** (for movement) or **pili** (for attaching to surfaces).
- Small, usually about 1–10 µm.

**Eukaryotic cells** (animals, plants, fungi and protists) have a **nucleus** and **membrane-bound organelles** such as mitochondria. Their DNA is linear, found in several chromosomes, and is wrapped around proteins. They are usually much bigger, about 10–100 µm.

| Feature | Prokaryotic | Eukaryotic |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | No (nucleoid region) | Yes, membrane-bound |
| Membrane-bound organelles | No | Yes |
| DNA | Circular, plus plasmids | Linear, in several chromosomes |
| Ribosomes | Smaller | Larger |
| Typical size | 1–10 µm | 10–100 µm |
| Examples | Bacteria, archaea | Animals, plants, fungi, protists |

The word 'prokaryote' roughly means 'before nucleus', and 'eukaryote' means 'true nucleus', which is a handy way to remember the difference.

### Plant cells and animal cells

Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic, so they share a nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and ribosomes. They differ in a few important ways, and each difference links to how the organism lives.

| Feature | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Yes, made of cellulose | No |
| Chloroplasts | Yes (in green parts) | No |
| Vacuole | One large central vacuole | Small, temporary vacuoles if any |
| Shape | Fairly fixed, often box-like | Flexible, varied |
| Centrioles | Absent in most plants | Present |

- The **cell wall** gives support. Plants have no skeleton, so rigid walls plus water pressure keep them upright.
- **Chloroplasts** carry out photosynthesis, so plants make their own food.
- The large **central vacuole** stores water and pushes the cytoplasm against the wall, keeping the cell firm.

Fungal cells also have a cell wall, but it is made of chitin, not cellulose, and they have no chloroplasts.

### Surface area to volume ratio

A cell must take in nutrients and oxygen and get rid of wastes, and all of this passes through its plasma membrane. The **surface area** (SA) is how much membrane is available for exchange. The **volume** (V) is how much cytoplasm needs to be supplied. The **surface area to volume ratio** (SA:V) compares the two.

As a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area. Volume scales with length cubed, but surface area only scales with length squared. So a large cell has relatively less membrane to serve each unit of cytoplasm. Materials also have further to travel to reach the centre. This is the main reason cells stay small, and why big organisms are made of many small cells rather than one huge cell.

Cells and organisms increase SA:V in several ways:

- Staying small, or dividing when they get too big.
- Being long and thin or flat (for example, red blood cells are flattened discs).
- Folding the membrane into **microvilli**, tiny finger-like projections, like those on cells lining the small intestine.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Calculating SA:V for cubes

A student models cells as cubes with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm. Which has the highest SA:V?

Step 1. For a cube with side length L: SA = 6 × L², and V = L³.

Step 2. Work through each cube.

| Side (cm) | SA (cm²) | V (cm³) | SA:V |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6 × 1 = 6 | 1 | 6 : 1 |
| 2 | 6 × 4 = 24 | 8 | 3 : 1 |
| 4 | 6 × 16 = 96 | 64 | 1.5 : 1 |

Step 3. Interpret. The 1 cm cube has 6 cm² of surface for every 1 cm³ of volume, while the 4 cm cube has only 1.5 cm². Each time the side doubles, SA:V halves. The smallest cube would exchange materials most efficiently.

### Example 2: Same volume, different shape

Compare a cube of side 2 cm with a flat block measuring 4 cm × 4 cm × 0.5 cm.

Step 1. Volumes. Cube: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Flat block: 4 × 4 × 0.5 = 8 cm³. Same volume.

Step 2. Surface areas. Cube: 6 × 4 = 24 cm². Flat block has two faces of 4 × 4 = 16 cm² and four faces of 4 × 0.5 = 2 cm², so SA = 32 + 8 = 40 cm².

Step 3. Ratios. Cube: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 : 1. Flat block: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 : 1.

Step 4. Conclusion. Flattening a cell increases SA:V without changing its volume. This explains why red blood cells, which must exchange oxygen quickly, are flattened discs.

### Example 3: Identifying a cell

An unknown cell is 3 µm long, has a cell wall, ribosomes and a ring of DNA, but no nucleus. It must be prokaryotic: the lack of a nucleus is the deciding feature. The cell wall does not tell you it is a plant cell, because bacteria and fungi also have cell walls.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking prokaryotes have no DNA or no ribosomes. They have both; they just lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
- Using 'has a cell wall' to prove a cell is a plant cell. Bacteria and fungi have walls too. Chloroplasts or a cellulose wall are better clues.
- Saying all plant cells have chloroplasts. Root cells, for example, usually do not.
- Saying a bigger cell has a bigger SA:V. A bigger cell has a bigger surface area, but a smaller ratio.
- Forgetting units or mixing them, for example dividing cm² by mm³.

## Exam tips

- SA:V questions often give you dimensions and ask you to calculate and then explain. Full marks need both the numbers and the link: lower SA:V means slower exchange of materials per unit of volume.
- When comparing cell types, write in matched pairs, for example 'prokaryotes lack a nucleus whereas eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus'. Listing features of only one cell type rarely earns full marks.
- In 'identify the cell' questions, name the specific feature that proves your answer.

## Tips to remember

- **"Pro = No, Eu = Do"**: **pro**karyotes have **no** nucleus; **eu**karyotes **do**.
- **"My Cat Really Dances"** for the four things every cell has: plasma **M**embrane, **C**ytosol, **R**ibosomes, **D**NA. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Plant cells' three Cs**: **C**ellulose cell wall, **C**hloroplasts and a **C**entral vacuole. (A made-up memory trick.) A wall alone does not prove a plant cell, because bacteria and fungi have walls too.
- **Crushed ice melts faster than a block**: lots of small pieces have far more surface for their volume, just like small cells exchange materials faster than big ones.
- **Double the side, halve the ratio**: cubes of 1, 2 and 4 cm give SA:V of 6 : 1, 3 : 1 and 1.5 : 1. Bigger cell = bigger surface area, but smaller ratio.

## Key terms

- **Cell theory** — the idea that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
- **Prokaryotic cell** — a cell without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles (bacteria and archaea).
- **Eukaryotic cell** — a cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
- **Nucleoid** — the region of a prokaryotic cell where the chromosome is found.
- **Plasmid** — a small, circular piece of DNA separate from the main chromosome, common in bacteria.
- **Cell wall** — a rigid layer outside the plasma membrane that gives support (cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, peptidoglycan in bacteria).
- **Surface area to volume ratio (SA:V)** — the surface area of a cell divided by its volume; a measure of how well it can exchange materials.
- **Microvilli** — tiny folds of the plasma membrane that increase surface area.

## Summary

- Cell theory: all living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and all cells come from existing cells.
- All cells have a plasma membrane, cytosol, ribosomes and DNA.
- Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both and are usually much bigger.
- Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; animal cells do not.
- As a cell grows, its SA:V falls, so exchange of materials becomes less efficient. This limits cell size.
- Cells increase SA:V by staying small, flattening or folding their membranes.

questions.prompt: Which statement is part of cell theory?

options.B: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
options.C: All living things are made of many cells.
options.D: Cells can form from non-living matter under the right conditions.

questions.explanation: Cell theory states that new cells only arise from the division of existing cells. C is tempting, but cell theory says living things are made of one OR more cells, so single-celled organisms count. A is wrong because prokaryotes have no nucleus, and D describes spontaneous generation, which cell theory rejects.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: All cells need ribosomes to make proteins, so both groups have them (prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller). Mitochondria (B) are tempting because all cells release energy, but prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles. The nucleus and ER are also only found in eukaryotes.

questions.prompt: A cell is 2 µm long, has a cell wall, a circular chromosome and plasmids, and no membrane-bound organelles. This cell is most likely
questions.explanation: No membrane-bound organelles, a circular chromosome, plasmids and a tiny size all point to a prokaryote such as a bacterium. B and C are tempting because they have cell walls, but plant and fungal cells are eukaryotic, with a nucleus and organelles.

questions.prompt: Which feature would best show that a cell came from a plant rather than an animal or a fungus?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells (and some protists) but never in animal or fungal cells. A cell wall (B) is the tempting answer, but fungi and bacteria also have walls, so it does not prove the cell is from a plant. A nucleus and mitochondria are found in all three.

questions.prompt: Why do cells usually stay small?

options.A: Large cells cannot fit enough DNA in their nucleus.
options.B: As a cell grows, its surface area increases faster than its volume.
options.C: As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so exchange becomes less efficient.
options.D: Larger cells have a higher surface area to volume ratio, which causes them to lose too much water.

questions.explanation: Volume grows with length cubed while surface area grows with length squared, so a growing cell has less membrane per unit of cytoplasm to exchange materials. B reverses the relationship, and D is wrong because larger cells have a LOWER SA:V, not a higher one.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped cell model has sides of 3 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: SA = 6 × 3² = 54 cm² and V = 3³ = 27 cm³, so SA:V = 54 ÷ 27 = 2 : 1. D (6 : 1) is the ratio for a 1 cm cube, a common answer if you forget to square and cube the side length. C has the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: Two cell models have the same volume of 8 cm³. Model X is a 2 cm cube. Model Y is a flat block, 4 cm × 4 cm × 0.5 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both models have the same SA:V because they have the same volume.
options.B: Model X has the higher SA:V because it is more compact.
options.C: Model Y has a surface area of 32 cm² and an SA:V of 4 : 1.
options.D: Model Y has the higher SA:V, 5 : 1 compared with 3 : 1 for model X.

questions.explanation: Model X: SA = 24 cm², ratio 24 ÷ 8 = 3 : 1. Model Y: SA = (2 × 16) + (4 × 2) = 40 cm², ratio 40 ÷ 8 = 5 : 1. C is tempting if you only count the two large faces (32 cm²) and forget the four thin edges. A is wrong because shape changes surface area even when volume stays the same.

questions.prompt: Cells lining the small intestine have many microvilli on the surface facing the gut. The main advantage of microvilli is that they

options.A: increase the volume of the cell so it can store more nutrients.
options.B: increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients without greatly increasing volume.
options.C: decrease the surface area to volume ratio so less water is lost.
options.D: act as a cell wall to protect the cell from digestive enzymes.

questions.explanation: Microvilli are folds of the plasma membrane that add a lot of surface area while adding very little volume, so SA:V rises and absorption is faster. A is tempting, but the benefit is extra membrane for exchange, not extra storage space. Microvilli increase SA:V, so C is the opposite of the truth.
